channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Exercise may be good for your social life, studies in mice suggest
item.description: If you've been thinking about joining one of the social running, walking or hiking clubs popping up on your social media feeds, new research from The Ohio State University offers another reason to give it a try: Working out with other people might serve as a social lubricant.

item.title: US loses measles elimination status as knowledge gaps about disease and vaccine persist
item.description: As the United States loses its status as a country that has eliminated measles, a new nationally representative Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) survey finds many Americans still lack basic knowledge about the disease and the vaccine that prevents it.

item.title: Small changes can make for a healthier holiday season
item.description: As the holidays approach, Pennington Biomedical Research Center is sharing practical tips to help families enjoy their holiday traditions while maintaining healthy habits. From making mindful food choices to finding opportunities for physical activity, experts say a few small changes can help people navigate the season without sacrificing the foods and traditions they enjoy.

item.title: Researchers find two understudied 'forever chemicals' raise liver cancer risk
item.description: A first-of-its-kind USC study links two little-studied "forever chemicals" to liver cancer, with the greatest risk in those already genetically susceptible to fatty liver disease. The study, published in Environmental Health Perspectives, finds that two per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as "forever chemicals," are associated with a significantly higher risk of liver cancer, with the strongest effects in people genetically predisposed to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), also known as fatty liver disease.

item.title: New 'atlas' of rare lung disease may help researchers develop improved treatments
item.description: When women develop the hard-to-pronounce lung disease called lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a natural set of brakes on cell growth fails inside their lungs, causing affected cells to form cysts that can threaten their ability to breathe.

item.title: Sugar made by gut bacterium may help the body burn visceral fat
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a sugar produced by a gut bacterium can increase energy burning in visceral fat—the harmful fat that accumulates around internal organs—while reducing weight gain and improving metabolic health, offering a potential new approach to tackling obesity.

item.title: Antibody-drug conjugate shows promising early results in Phase I trial in sarcoma patients
item.description: An antibody-drug conjugate, a type of drug that targets and enters cancer cells like a Trojan Horse, has shown promising early results across diverse types of soft tissue sarcoma in a Phase I trial. The findings were presented at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

item.title: Mexico launches anti-measles drive after losing eradication status
item.description: Mexico on Wednesday launched a 90-day "rapid response plan" against an ongoing outbreak of measles that has caused the country to lose its eradication status for the highly contagious disease.

item.title: Neurosteroid offers clues to brain changes linked to depression
item.description: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers and colleagues, including two at UT Dallas, have found evidence that pregnenolone—a naturally occurring steroid hormone the body produces from cholesterol—may alter patterns of communication between key brain regions involved in depression and cognitive control.

item.title: Changes needed to allow more GPs to attend aged care facilities
item.description: Attendance by general practitioners (GPs) at aged care facilities is a crucial health care concern, with an increasing number of Australians living permanently in residential aged care, and South Australia recording the highest rate—44 people per 1,000.

item.title: Two measures to help prevent obesity in young people
item.description: Obesity in children and young people increases the risk of health problems later in life to such an extent that tackling it is important, both for individuals and for the population as a whole. The condition is generally linked to diet and lifestyle. A new study including almost 125,000 children examines how best to help parents and children make healthier choices. The paper is published in the journal Acta Paediatrica.

item.title: Home-based auricular vagus nerve stimulation shows early promise for kids and teens with migraines
item.description: As clinicians and researchers, we often see how heavily migraine attacks weigh on children and adolescents, yet non-pharmacological, child-friendly treatment options remain strikingly scarce. For years, our team at Nanfang Hospital and collaborating institutes have been looking into ways to bridge this gap.

item.title: New evidence questions benefits of turmeric for knee arthritis
item.description: A new Cochrane review has found that turmeric supplements may provide little or no clinically important pain relief for people with knee osteoarthritis, challenging conclusions from earlier research that suggested a benefit. The work appears in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

item.title: Analysis of over 69,000 younger patients questions one-size-fits-all cutoff for colorectal cancer stool test
item.description: A new study led by experts at the University of Nottingham has provided new insight into how a commonly used test for colorectal cancer performs in people under 50.

item.title: How research paved the way for progress in a rare form of ALS
item.description: An experimental ALS drug that grew out of basic and clinical research at Columbia University's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons may soon become available for patients with a rare and aggressive form of the disease.

item.title: No clear benefit from two drugs intended to increase spontaneous birth after induction in first-time moms
item.description: There is no clear evidence that hyoscine butylbromide or sodium bicarbonate improves spontaneous vaginal birth rates (without the assistance of forceps or vacuum) in first-time moms after induction of labor, finds a large Norwegian trial published by The BMJ. Although small benefits of either drug can't be entirely ruled out, the researchers say the findings do not support their routine use.

item.title: Use of AI in medical recruitment could miss top talent, doctors warn
item.description: As NHS England prepares to introduce a £1.2 billion AI-driven workforce management and recruitment platform, a new report from BMJ Careers raises concerns about quality, fairness and missing top talent as medical recruiters respond to a flood of AI-powered applications.

item.title: Morphea linked to higher risk for cancer
item.description: Morphea is associated with excess cancer incidence, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: Most children labeled allergic to antibiotics may not have an allergy, researchers warn
item.description: It's 7 p.m. on a Saturday in an urgent care center. A 10-year-old boy is "really sick" with severe tonsillitis and clearly needs antibiotics. Just before I (Rebecca Payne) head out to find a suitable medicine, I ask his mother: "Does he have any allergies?"

item.title: Creatine supplement use nearly doubles among US college students, new study finds
item.description: The use of creatine and protein supplements among U.S. college and university students has increased significantly over a five-year period, according to new research published in the journal Performance Enhancement & Health and led by researchers at the University of Toronto.

item.title: How to relieve a stress headache (and keep the next one away)
item.description: You had a rough day at work and got stuck in traffic on the way home, and suddenly your head starts to ache.

item.title: Brepocitinib yields improvements in cutaneous sarcoidosis
item.description: For patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis (CS), brepocitinib is associated with dose-dependent and clinically meaningful improvements, according to a study published online in JAMA Dermatology to coincide with the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

item.title: Noninvasive deep brain stimulation improves subclinical depression, study finds
item.description: Researchers led by professor Tu Yiheng from the Institute of Psychology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Shenzhen University and other institutions, have developed a noninvasive deep brain stimulation approach that enhances reward learning and improves depressive symptoms in individuals with subclinical depression.

item.title: Your brain may be hiding Alzheimer's from you—and that's not always a good thing
item.description: When scientists examine the brains of older people after death, what they find can often be puzzling. One such puzzle is that around a third of people who showed no signs of dementia when they were alive had brains that contained key indicators of Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: FDA approves drug for infantile-onset Niemann-Pick type C after analysis finds longer survival
item.description: Researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and their collaborators at Beren Therapeutics, Thousand Oaks, California, have developed a treatment for infants with Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) disease, which is a rare and rapidly fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disorder. The drug, known as cyclodextrin (brand name Adrabetadex), extended the survival of participants with NPC in a large, international clinical trial and represents foundational scientific research efforts that began 20 years ago. The drug was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.title: Targeting immune overactivity in Down syndrome shows promise in phase 2 clinical trial
item.description: In a first-of-its-kind clinical trial, researchers at the Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome (Crnic Institute) at the University of Colorado Anschutz found that a medication targeting immune overactivity in people with Down syndrome reduced underlying inflammation and was associated with improvements in inflammatory skin conditions, while opening new avenues for research on brain health and Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: Acupuncture‑like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
item.description: A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.

item.title: Blood test may reveal which lymphoma patients will respond to immunotherapy
item.description: Cornell engineers and Dana-Farber oncologists found that RNA floating in the plasma carries a signature of a lymphoma tumor's surroundings, one that tracked with whether patients were still in remission a year later.

item.title: Milkshake study offers clues to diet's brain effects in young adults
item.description: Results from a Virginia Tech eating trial add to evidence that the developing brain responds differently to foods that have been through industrial processing or contain ingredients not found in a home kitchen.

item.title: Migraine and smoking associated with increased risk of stroke by age 60
item.description: Migraine and smoking were each associated with a higher risk of early stroke in people who had given birth, while participants with both had the highest risk, according to a study published in Neurology. The study defined early stroke as occurring at age 60 or younger.
